script.opening: “She’s been sent home from school again. That’s twice this month. I’ve tried everything they sell at the chemist and they keep coming back. I need the proper strong stuff on prescription, because I can’t keep paying for it.”

facts.text: Kerry (mother) with Maisie, 8, on the sofa beside her. Maisie is quiet and looks down. Kerry is tired and talks fast.

facts.topic: How long and what was used
facts.text: About three months. Four different products from the chemist: “a spray, two lotions and a shampoo one”. Each used once. She did not know about repeating after a week. One was put on wet hair and washed out after 10 minutes because Maisie said it stung. She has a detection comb but “it takes forever, and Maisie screams”.

facts.topic: Only if asked what else she has tried
facts.text: Last Saturday she sprayed Maisie’s hair with the dog’s flea spray: “It kills fleas, so I thought…”. Since then Maisie’s scalp has been sore and a bit red at the back. No vomiting, no drowsiness, no breathing problems. The bottle is in the kitchen.

Maisie stays every other weekend at her dad’s with his partner and two stepbrothers, 10 and 12. Kerry and the father communicate “by text, when he answers”. As far as she knows nobody there has been checked or treated. Lice come back after those weekends.

The head teacher phoned and said Maisie must stay at home “until she is clear”. She has missed four days. A few children call her “nitty” and won’t sit with her. She cried this morning and said she doesn’t want to go back.

Kerry works two part-time jobs (cleaning and a supermarket). Has spent about £60 on products. Feels judged by the school and by other mums. Maisie is otherwise well, with no asthma, eczema or allergies, no medicines. Kerry is not pregnant.

Defensive at first: “I’m not a dirty mum.” Softens a lot if the doctor says clearly this is not about hygiene and that she has clearly tried hard. Brings up the flea spray only if asked what else she has tried, then looks embarrassed. Very relieved to hear Maisie can be in school, and grateful if the doctor offers to put this in writing.

ice.ideas: “These lice must be resistant to everything. She needs something stronger that only a doctor can give.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: money is very tight and she cannot afford another product; she thinks the school sees her as a neglectful mother and she is frightened social services will be called. She also feels guilty about the flea spray.
ice.expectations: “A prescription for the strong stuff, and a letter so the school stops sending her home.”

cues: “I’ve tried everything” — find out exactly what and how; most failures are technique, a missed repeat or reinfestation.
Maisie looking down and the school sending her home — her distress and the bullying matter.
“I can’t keep paying for it” — cost; the self-care policy allows prescribing where social vulnerability limits self-care.
Embarrassed pause when asked what else she has tried — the dog flea spray.

checkpoints.text: Takes a precise treatment history: which products, how applied, how long left on, whether repeated after 7 days, whether detection combing was used to check for cure
Asks what else has been tried and identifies the veterinary flea spray; checks for scalp irritation and systemic symptoms, and advises stopping it and washing it out
Identifies reinfestation from the second household (father’s house) as a likely cause of failure, and checks how lice were confirmed (live lice found on combing)

Plans a physically acting treatment used correctly (for example dimeticone 4%: dry hair, whole scalp, left for the time in the product information, repeated after 7 days; check the SPC/product information), or structured wet combing, with detection combing 2–3 days after finishing and again a week later
Coordinates checking of everyone in both households with treatment of anyone with live lice on the same day, and suggests a practical way to involve the father
Corrects the school exclusion: UKHSA guidance sets no exclusion for head lice; offers a letter and/or contact with the school nurse, and raises the bullying with the school
Makes a reasoned prescribing decision, using the national self-care guidance exception for significant social vulnerability, and explains it
Removes stigma early, acknowledges the mother’s effort without judging the flea spray, involves Maisie directly, and safety-nets for a worsening scalp or treatment failure

worked.txt: “Before anything else: head lice have nothing to do with being a clean or dirty home. You have clearly tried hard, and it’s exhausting. Let’s work out why it keeps coming back.”

“Talk me through each product. How long did you leave it on? Did you do it again a week later? Most of the time it isn’t resistance — it’s that the eggs hatch after the first go, or the lice come back from somewhere else.”

“Thank you for telling me. Products for dogs aren’t safe on children’s skin, so please don’t use it again and wash her hair through with plain shampoo tonight. Has she been sick, drowsy or had any breathing trouble?”

“The weekends at her dad’s are the gap. Everyone in both houses needs combing on the same evening, and anyone with live lice treated the same day. Would it help if I put that in writing for you to send him?”
“Maisie doesn’t need to be off school. The national guidance for schools says no exclusion for head lice. I’m happy to write that down, and I’d like the school nurse to know about the name-calling.”

“I’ll prescribe a lotion that works by coating the lice, so resistance doesn’t matter. Put it on dry hair, leave it for the full time on the pack, and repeat exactly 7 days later. Then comb her wet hair 2–3 days after the second go and again a week later to make sure they’ve gone.”

f.learning: Persistent head lice are rarely due to “super-resistant” lice. Most treatment failures come from incorrect use (wet hair, too short a contact time, too little product), a missed 7-day repeat application, or reinfestation from untreated close contacts, often a second household. Take a precise treatment history and ask what else has been tried: parents under pressure sometimes use unsafe remedies such as veterinary insecticides, paraffin or undiluted essential oils. Stop them, wash the hair, and check for skin irritation and systemic symptoms (advice is available from NHS 111, or for clinicians through TOXBASE/NPIS). Diagnosis and cure are confirmed by detection combing for live lice. A physically acting product such as dimeticone 4% avoids insecticide resistance; it must be applied to dry hair over the whole scalp, left for the full time in the product information and repeated after 7 days (check the SPC/product information), with detection combing 2–3 days after finishing and again a week later. Structured wet combing is the alternative. Check everyone in each household the child lives in, and treat only those with live lice, on the same day. UKHSA guidance for schools and childcare settings sets no exclusion for head lice, so a GP can support the child’s return and raise any bullying with the school or school nurse. National self-care guidance means head-lice products are usually bought over the counter, but it allows prescribing where significant social vulnerability limits self-care. The skills are a non-judgemental treatment-failure analysis, spotting the safety issue, involving the child, and practical help across two households and the school.

knowledge.summary: Repeated head-lice infestation over three months, with four products each used once and incorrectly, reinfestation from an untreated second household, an unsafe veterinary insecticide on the child’s scalp, wrongful exclusion from school with bullying, and a stretched parent. Find the causes of failure, stop the flea spray and check for harm, prescribe a physically acting treatment with clear instructions and the 7-day repeat, coordinate both households, correct the exclusion, and support Maisie and her mother without judgement.

points.t: Common causes: product applied to wet hair or rinsed early, too little product, no repeat after 7 days (eggs hatch after the first application), and reinfestation from close contacts who were not checked [1]. True resistance is mainly a problem with neurotoxic insecticides.
Diagnosis and cure need a live louse found by detection combing of wet, conditioned hair. Itch can persist for some days after successful treatment and is not proof of failure.

Dimeticone 4% coats the lice, so insecticide resistance does not apply. Apply to dry hair from scalp to tips, leave for the time stated in the product information, wash out, and repeat after 7 days (check the SPC/product information). Check for cure with detection combing 2–3 days after the second application and again a week later [1].

Structured combing of wet, conditioned hair with a detection comb every few days for at least two weeks, continuing until no live lice are seen at consecutive sessions. Useful where products are not wanted or tolerated.

Veterinary insecticides, paraffin and undiluted essential oils should not be used on children. Wash the hair through, look for skin irritation or burns, and ask about vomiting, drowsiness, twitching or breathing problems. Clinicians can get poisons advice through TOXBASE or the National Poisons Information Service.

Check everyone in each household the child lives in, including a second parent’s home, on the same evening. Treat only those with live lice, on the same day. No need to wash all bedding or treat pets.
UKHSA guidance [2]: no exclusion period for head lice. A child should not be sent home or kept off. The GP can provide a letter, involve the school nurse and raise bullying with the school.

Head-lice products are on the national list of items for self-care purchase [3], but the guidance includes a general exception where a clinician judges that medical, mental health or significant social vulnerability compromises self-care. Record the reason.

Persistent head lice in a family that is actively trying to treat them is not, on its own, neglect. Look at the whole picture: the child’s wellbeing, school attendance, bullying and the parent’s capacity. Offer early help if the family would value it [6].

dg.d: Open question to both; named the stigma early and set the agenda: why treatment fails, school, cost.
Two households, single parent with two jobs, money, Maisie’s experience of bullying and missed school.
Remote look at the scalp for irritation or infection; detection combing as the test for live lice and for cure.
Incorrect use, missed repeat and reinfestation versus true resistance; irritant reaction to the flea spray versus secondary infection.
Asked about vomiting, drowsiness, twitching and breathing after the insecticide; neck glands; crusting or weeping.
Persistent head lice due to incorrect use and reinfestation, plus a scalp irritant reaction to a veterinary product.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Stop the flea spray; dimeticone used correctly with the 7-day repeat (check the SPC/product information); check for cure by combing; both households on the same evening.
School letter and no exclusion; bullying raised with the school nurse; prescribing under the social vulnerability exception; note for the father.
Teach-back; combing checks after treatment; return if lice persist or the scalp worsens; NHS 111 if unwell after the spray; early help offered.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Followed the pause about ‘what else’ to the flea spray; noticed Maisie looking down and asked her directly.
Idea (resistant lice need something stronger), concerns (cost, being judged, social services), expectation (prescription and a school letter).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — money is very tight and she cannot afford another product; she thinks the school sees her as a neglectful mother and she is frightened social services will be called. She also feels guilty about the flea spray — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Clarke. Hello Maisie, and you must be Mum. What’s been happening?

She’s been sent home from school again. That’s twice this month. I’ve tried everything they sell at the chemist and they keep coming back. I need the proper strong stuff on prescription, because I can’t keep paying for it.

That sounds exhausting, and I can see you’ve really been trying. One thing first, because people often worry about it: head lice have nothing to do with a clean or dirty home. Any child can get them. Let’s work out why they keep coming back.
The school makes me feel like I’m a dirty mum.
I’m sorry you’ve been made to feel that way. Can you talk me through each product you used, how you put it on, and how long you left it?
A spray, two lotions and a shampoo one. Once each. One I put on after her bath and washed off after ten minutes because she said it stung.
Did any of them say to do it again a week later?
I didn’t know you had to. I thought one go killed them.

That’s really common, and it’s the main reason lice seem to come back. The lotion kills the lice but not always the eggs, so new ones hatch in the following week. Have you been able to comb her hair to check for live ones?

model.text: I’ve got a comb, but it takes forever and she screams.
Has anything else been tried, maybe something from home? People try all sorts when they’re desperate, and I won’t judge.

No, she’s been fine, just the sore bit at the back.
Could you tip the camera so I can see the back of her scalp? I can see a patch of redness but no blisters, weeping or crusting. Can you feel any lumps in her neck?

model.text: No lumps.

Products for dogs are made for animal skin and aren’t safe for children, so please don’t use it again. Wash her hair through with ordinary shampoo tonight. If she becomes unwell, sick or drowsy, ring 111 straight away and keep the bottle to show them.
Where does Maisie spend her time? Is there anywhere else she sleeps?
Every other weekend at her dad’s. He’s got two stepsons. They come back after those weekends, now you mention it.
Maisie, can I ask you something? How have things been at school?
(Maisie) Some people call me nitty. I don’t want to go back.
That sounds horrible, Maisie, and it isn’t fair. Mum, what are you most worried about with all this?
Honestly? That the school thinks I can’t look after her and they’ll call social services. And money. I’ve spent sixty quid.

Lots of families get stuck in this loop, and it doesn’t mean you can’t look after her. Here’s my plan. I’ll prescribe a lotion called dimeticone. It works by coating the lice rather than poisoning them, so they can’t be resistant to it. It goes on dry hair, the whole scalp from roots to tips, and stays on for the full time on the leaflet. Then exactly seven days later you do it again.
Normally these are bought from the chemist, but there’s an exception when cost and circumstances make that hard, and I think that applies here.
Thank you. What about her dad’s?

Everyone in both houses needs checking with the comb on the same evening, and anyone with live lice treated on the same day as Maisie. I can write a short note you can send her dad, so it doesn’t feel like it’s coming from you.

And school: national guidance says children with head lice should not be sent home or kept off. I’ll write a letter for you to take in, and with your agreement I’ll let the school nurse know about the name-calling so the school can deal with it.
I didn’t know that. They made it sound like the rules.
Can you tell me the plan back so I know I’ve explained it well?
No more flea spray. Lotion on dry hair, leave it on, again in a week. Comb everyone, here and at her dad’s, same night. She goes to school with your letter.

Perfect. Comb her wet hair two or three days after the second go and again a week after that. If you still find live lice, or her scalp gets weepy, crusty or more sore, book back with me. And if you ever want extra support at home, there’s help available, but nobody thinks you’re a bad mum.
model.why: Check for cure; safety-net; early help offered without judgement

social.t: Children who move between parents’ homes are often reinfested from the untreated household. A neutral note from the GP can help where parents find it hard to talk.
Repeated product purchases are a real burden on a low income. Shame makes parents less likely to ask for help or disclose unsafe remedies.

legal.t: NHS England’s guidance on over-the-counter items lists head-lice treatments for self-care, with a general exception where medical, mental health or significant social vulnerability compromises self-care. Record the reason.
UKHSA guidance for education and childcare settings sets no exclusion for head lice. Schools can ask parents to treat, but should not send children home.

professional.t: Asking what else has been tried, without blame, is how unsafe remedies come to light. Respond to the risk, not the parent’s choice.
Speak to the child directly. Bullying and missed school are part of the problem the consultation should address.

community.t: The school nursing service can support the family, give consistent advice to the school and help with bullying.
Pharmacists can demonstrate detection combing and product use, and may run local minor ailment schemes.

redFlags: Vomiting, drowsiness, twitching or breathing problems after a home insecticide: urgent assessment (NHS 111/999); poisons advice for clinicians via TOXBASE/NPIS
Weeping, crusted scalp with tender neck glands: secondary bacterial infection
Scalp scaling or patchy hair loss without lice: consider tinea capitis, eczema or psoriasis
psychosocial: Two households and communication with the father
Fear of being judged as neglectful
ice: Idea: the lice are resistant and need a stronger product
Concern: cost; being judged; social services
Expectation: a prescription and a letter for school

playbook.diagnosis: “This is head lice coming back because the treatments weren’t repeated and Maisie is being reinfested at her dad’s, not because the lice are super-resistant. The soreness at the back is irritation from the flea spray.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The lotion kills the lice but some eggs survive and hatch over the next week, which is why you repeat it. And if anyone she stays with still has lice, they simply walk back across.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve spent a lot, you feel judged, and you’re worried what the school thinks. You’ve done nothing wrong. Let’s fix the treatment and get her back in school.”
management.psychosocial: Remove shame; involve Maisie; tackle bullying through the school nurse; reduce cost; support the parents to coordinate.

pitfalls.intro: The lice are easy. The marks are in finding why treatment failed, spotting the unsafe remedy, and helping a stretched parent and an unhappy child without blame.

items.fail: Prescribing a stronger product without a treatment history.
items.why: Failure is usually technique, a missed repeat or reinfestation.
items.fix: Ask about each product, how it was used and whether it was repeated.

items.fail: Never asking what else has been tried.
items.why: The veterinary insecticide is a safety issue.
items.fix: Ask openly and without blame; check the scalp and for systemic symptoms.

items.why: Reinfestation from untreated contacts keeps the cycle going.
items.fix: Ask where the child sleeps; coordinate same-evening checks in both homes.

items.why: UKHSA guidance sets no exclusion for head lice.
items.fix: Offer a letter and involve the school nurse.

items.why: Maisie’s distress and bullying are part of the case.

items.fail: Shaming the mother about the flea spray or hinting at neglect.
items.why: She will disengage and stop disclosing.
items.fix: Thank her for telling you and focus on what to do next.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Repeated head-lice infestation over three months, with four products each used once and incorrectly, reinfestation from an untreated second household, an unsafe veterinary insecticide on the child’s scalp, wrongful exclusion from school with bullying, and a stretched parent. Find the causes of failure, stop the flea spray and check for harm, prescribe a physically acting treatment with clear instructions and the 7-day repeat, coordinate both households, correct the exclusion, and support Maisie and her mother without judgement.

points.t: Common causes: product applied to wet hair or rinsed early, too little product, no repeat after 7 days (eggs hatch after the first application), and reinfestation from close contacts who were not checked [1]. True resistance is mainly a problem with neurotoxic insecticides.
Diagnosis and cure need a live louse found by detection combing of wet, conditioned hair. Itch can persist for some days after successful treatment and is not proof of failure.

Dimeticone 4% coats the lice, so insecticide resistance does not apply. Apply to dry hair from scalp to tips, leave for the time stated in the product information, wash out, and repeat after 7 days (check the SPC/product information). Check for cure with detection combing 2–3 days after the second application and again a week later [1].

Structured combing of wet, conditioned hair with a detection comb every few days for at least two weeks, continuing until no live lice are seen at consecutive sessions. Useful where products are not wanted or tolerated.

Veterinary insecticides, paraffin and undiluted essential oils should not be used on children. Wash the hair through, look for skin irritation or burns, and ask about vomiting, drowsiness, twitching or breathing problems. Clinicians can get poisons advice through TOXBASE or the National Poisons Information Service.

Check everyone in each household the child lives in, including a second parent’s home, on the same evening. Treat only those with live lice, on the same day. No need to wash all bedding or treat pets.
UKHSA guidance [2]: no exclusion period for head lice. A child should not be sent home or kept off. The GP can provide a letter, involve the school nurse and raise bullying with the school.

Head-lice products are on the national list of items for self-care purchase [3], but the guidance includes a general exception where a clinician judges that medical, mental health or significant social vulnerability compromises self-care. Record the reason.

Persistent head lice in a family that is actively trying to treat them is not, on its own, neglect. Look at the whole picture: the child’s wellbeing, school attendance, bullying and the parent’s capacity. Offer early help if the family would value it [6].

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question to both; named the stigma early and set the agenda: why treatment fails, school, cost.
Two households, single parent with two jobs, money, Maisie’s experience of bullying and missed school.
Followed the pause about ‘what else’ to the flea spray; noticed Maisie looking down and asked her directly.
Idea (resistant lice need something stronger), concerns (cost, being judged, social services), expectation (prescription and a school letter).
Remote look at the scalp for irritation or infection; detection combing as the test for live lice and for cure.
Incorrect use, missed repeat and reinfestation versus true resistance; irritant reaction to the flea spray versus secondary infection.
Asked about vomiting, drowsiness, twitching and breathing after the insecticide; neck glands; crusting or weeping.
Persistent head lice due to incorrect use and reinfestation, plus a scalp irritant reaction to a veterinary product.
Stop the flea spray; dimeticone used correctly with the 7-day repeat (check the SPC/product information); check for cure by combing; both households on the same evening.
School letter and no exclusion; bullying raised with the school nurse; prescribing under the social vulnerability exception; note for the father.
Teach-back; combing checks after treatment; return if lice persist or the scalp worsens; NHS 111 if unwell after the spray; early help offered.

social.t: Children who move between parents’ homes are often reinfested from the untreated household. A neutral note from the GP can help where parents find it hard to talk.
Repeated product purchases are a real burden on a low income. Shame makes parents less likely to ask for help or disclose unsafe remedies.

legal.t: NHS England’s guidance on over-the-counter items lists head-lice treatments for self-care, with a general exception where medical, mental health or significant social vulnerability compromises self-care. Record the reason.
UKHSA guidance for education and childcare settings sets no exclusion for head lice. Schools can ask parents to treat, but should not send children home.

professional.t: Asking what else has been tried, without blame, is how unsafe remedies come to light. Respond to the risk, not the parent’s choice.
Speak to the child directly. Bullying and missed school are part of the problem the consultation should address.

community.t: The school nursing service can support the family, give consistent advice to the school and help with bullying.
Pharmacists can demonstrate detection combing and product use, and may run local minor ailment schemes.

redFlags: Vomiting, drowsiness, twitching or breathing problems after a home insecticide: urgent assessment (NHS 111/999); poisons advice for clinicians via TOXBASE/NPIS
Weeping, crusted scalp with tender neck glands: secondary bacterial infection
Scalp scaling or patchy hair loss without lice: consider tinea capitis, eczema or psoriasis
psychosocial: Two households and communication with the father
Fear of being judged as neglectful
ice: Idea: the lice are resistant and need a stronger product
Concern: cost; being judged; social services
Expectation: a prescription and a letter for school

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is head lice coming back because the treatments weren’t repeated and Maisie is being reinfested at her dad’s, not because the lice are super-resistant. The soreness at the back is irritation from the flea spray.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The lotion kills the lice but some eggs survive and hatch over the next week, which is why you repeat it. And if anyone she stays with still has lice, they simply walk back across.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve spent a lot, you feel judged, and you’re worried what the school thinks. You’ve done nothing wrong. Let’s fix the treatment and get her back in school.”
management.psychosocial: Remove shame; involve Maisie; tackle bullying through the school nurse; reduce cost; support the parents to coordinate.
sharedPlan: Stop the flea spray; wash the hair through with ordinary shampoo tonight
Dimeticone 4% on dry hair over the whole scalp, left for the full contact time, repeated after 7 days (check the SPC/product information)
Detection combing 2–3 days after the second application and again a week later
Comb everyone in both households on the same evening; treat anyone with live lice the same day
Letter for school: no exclusion (UKHSA); school nurse informed about bullying, with consent
Prescribed under the self-care exception for social vulnerability; reason recorded
safetyNet: NHS 111 or 999 if Maisie becomes sick, drowsy, twitchy or short of breath
Return if the scalp becomes weepy, crusted or more sore
Return if live lice are found after the second application

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The lice are easy. The marks are in finding why treatment failed, spotting the unsafe remedy, and helping a stretched parent and an unhappy child without blame.

items.fail: Prescribing a stronger product without a treatment history.
items.why: Failure is usually technique, a missed repeat or reinfestation.
items.fix: Ask about each product, how it was used and whether it was repeated.

items.fail: Never asking what else has been tried.
items.why: The veterinary insecticide is a safety issue.
items.fix: Ask openly and without blame; check the scalp and for systemic symptoms.

items.why: Reinfestation from untreated contacts keeps the cycle going.
items.fix: Ask where the child sleeps; coordinate same-evening checks in both homes.

items.why: UKHSA guidance sets no exclusion for head lice.
items.fix: Offer a letter and involve the school nurse.

items.why: Maisie’s distress and bullying are part of the case.

items.fail: Shaming the mother about the flea spray or hinting at neglect.
items.why: She will disengage and stop disclosing.
items.fix: Thank her for telling you and focus on what to do next.
